analysis.investment_thesis: PhysicsWallah's hyper-growth edtech story is real — ₹233 Cr to ₹2,887 Cr revenue in 3 years — but the company is still loss-making, has destroyed massive capital through impairments, and trades at an EV/EBITDA of 433x that even the most optimistic India bull cannot justify. Until sustained net profitability is demonstrated and valuation corrects sharply, this is speculation, not investment.
key_strengths: Explosive revenue CAGR of 131% (FY2022→FY2025) with OCF positive in all 4 years — the offline+hybrid model is working on cash generation
Strong promoter holding at 72.3% — founder-led with skin in the game, serving India's aspirational middle class at affordable price points
Operational recovery visible in FY2025: EBITDA turned to +₹234 Cr and FCF recovered to ₹340 Cr after the FY2024 disaster
key_risks: Valuation is unjustifiable — EV/EBITDA of 433x on a loss-making company; even at 5% net margin on ₹2,887 Cr revenue, P/E would be ~215x
FY2024 'other income' of -₹672 Cr signals massive impairment/writedowns, wiping equity to -₹1,246 Cr — classic sign of reckless acquisition spending during growth phase
EdTech sector is a graveyard — BYJU's destruction of capital is a sector-wide cautionary tale; offline expansion requires sustained capex with uncertain unit economics
red_flags: Equity turned deeply negative (-₹1,246 Cr in FY2024) — technically insolvent before IPO proceeds rescued the balance sheet; borrowings ballooned to ₹2,461 Cr
₹672 Cr of impairments/negative other income in FY2024 reveals poor capital allocation — management burned pre-IPO money on bad acquisitions
Net loss for 3 consecutive years despite revenue tripling — losses narrowed to -₹243 Cr in FY2025 but no clear timeline to sustainable net profitability
Cash on hand is a negligible ₹54 Cr against ₹997 Cr total debt — liquidity cushion is dangerously thin for a growth company still burning capital
analysis.detailed_analysis:
PhysicsWallah's revenue trajectory is genuinely one of the most impressive in recent Indian IPO history — scaling from ₹233 Cr to ₹2,887 Cr in just 3 years represents true disruption of the coaching market. The affordable pricing model, the two-teacher hybrid center format, and the brand built on YouTube credibility are real competitive advantages that differentiate PWL from the BYJU's playbook of aggressive debt-fuelled marketing. OCF has been positive in all 4 years (₹507 Cr in FY2025), and FCF recovering to ₹340 Cr tells me the underlying business mechanics are sound. This is not a fraud — it is a genuine business serving a real need in India's education-hungry middle class.

However, as Jhunjhunwala, I cannot overlook the capital destruction that preceded the IPO. The company burned through ₹1,131 Cr in net losses in FY2024, driven largely by ₹672 Cr in what appear to be impairments — clear evidence that management made poor acquisition decisions when capital was cheap. The balance sheet had to be rescued by the IPO. Now the market prices this company at ₹30,976 Cr — a 10.7x revenue multiple and EV/EBITDA of 433x — for a business still reporting net losses. I have built wealth by being patient and buying great businesses at fair prices. PWL may become a great business, but I need to see 2–3 years of consistent net profitability and a valuation closer to 25–40x earnings before this deserves a serious look. At INR 108, the market is pricing perfection into a company with an imperfect track record.
